docs.title: Home
docs.text:
Pre-release software

This project is in a pre-release state. The API is subject to change, and breaking changes may occur without notice.

docs.title: What does it stand for?
docs.text: eXtensible Agent Harness—or perhaps “Not Another Harness!”

docs.title: How is it pronounced?
docs.text: The a is silent.

docs.title: Should I use xah?
docs.text: xah is for people comfortable with Python development—directly or via agents—who want fine-grained control over how their agents behave.

docs.title: Who might find it useful?
docs.text:
xah may be useful if you want to:

  • Work with locally hosted models, whose tool discipline may not always be reliable.
  • Add custom tools—for example, ensure the agent can only run the right version of Python.
  • Add validation that blocks misbehavior even when prompts asking the agent not to do something have failed.
  • Add tools that aren't typically available in existing harnesses.
  • Subclass or extend existing tools, validation workflows, or subagents.
  • Extend agents to non-coding workflows.

docs.title: Who is xah not for?
docs.text:
• If you use frontier models exclusively and they already behave roughly how you want, a mainstream off-the-shelf agent may be a better fit.
  • If you do not want to work in Python or maintain code-level customizations, xah's main strength—extending the harness in Python—may not be useful to you.

docs.title: Why does xah exist?
docs.text: There are two main motivations for xah: extensibility, and adapting ACP for agents beyond coding.

docs.title: Extensibility
docs.text:
Existing harnesses can be limiting when a developer—or an agent working with them—needs to develop tools in a fine-grained, debuggable way. Common approaches tend to fall into a few groups:

  • Instructions: add more context in files such as AGENTS.md or skills, then hope the agent follows it.
  • Configuration: set coarse-grained options for behavior and permissions.
  • Plugin systems: gain more power, but learn a separate workflow; plugins can also be difficult to debug when they run through the agent.

These approaches have their place, but they aren't a substitute for being able to change the harness directly. xah makes it straightforward to develop and debug custom tools and validation as Python code. A prompt can ask an agent not to misbehave; code can block it from doing so.

xah is built on Pydantic AI and Pydantic Deep Agents.

docs.title: Adapting ACP for non-coding agents
docs.text:
The Agent Client Protocol (ACP) is designed to connect coding agents with clients such as editors and IDEs. It provides a standard communication interface, rather than a bespoke integration for every agent and client. ACP is not an agent-to-agent coordination protocol.

xah begins with the familiar coding-agent use case—an IDE, terminal UI, or similar client—and explores using that client experience with agents for other kinds of work, too.

docs.title: Get started
docs.text:
Install xah from PyPI and start the server:

pip install xah
xah

For an ephemeral run, use uvx xah. The server needs an ACP client for the interactive interface. See the quick start and PyCharm or Zed setup instructions, then work through the tutorials to extend xah.

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text: Visit the xah documentation for setup, ACP client configuration, tutorials, and agent data and skills.

docs.title: Get started
docs.text: New to xah? Start with the quick start, then work through the tutorials.

docs.title: Connect an ACP client
docs.text:
xah separates the agent server from its client. The server runs the agent; an ACP client provides the interface where you start a session, send prompts, and read replies. Most clients are IDEs or code editors, but terminal and web interfaces are also available.

The server and client are separate

Start the xah server first. An IDE's ACP configuration starts a small xah acp proxy that connects to that server; it does not start the server itself.

docs.title: Other client options
docs.text:
• ACP UI is a cross-platform chat client for desktop, mobile, and web. Its browser and mobile versions connect to remote agents over WebSocket. They cannot launch local stdio agents directly; exposing a local agent may require a WebSocket bridge.
  • ACP Web Gateway provides a browser interface through a gateway. Its documented setup relays an agent's ACP stdio connection over WebSocket; follow that project's instructions to run the gateway and agent.

These are third-party projects with their own setup and transport requirements. The IDE setup below connects the xah proxy to the local server directly.

docs.title: Start the server and connect a client
docs.text:
1. Install xah and start its server:

    pip install xah
xah

    The default HTTP address is http://localhost:8010; the ACP WebSocket endpoint is ws://localhost:8010/acp/ws. 2. Configure your ACP client to launch xah acp --url=ws://localhost:8010/acp/ws. 3. Use xah from the client's agent or chat interface. Keep the server running while you use the proxy.

docs.title: Use an IDE as your ACP client
docs.text:
In each editor, add the configuration for an ACP agent. The command and args start xah's stdio proxy; the server must already be running. Follow the editor's setup flow to open the right configuration file.

PyCharmZed

JetBrains stores custom agents in the user-level ~/.jetbrains/acp.json. Open AI Chat, choose Add Custom Agent, and add this entry to agent_servers, preserving other entries:

{
  "default_mcp_settings": {},
  "agent_servers": {
    "xah": {
      "command": "xah",
      "args": [
        "acp",
        "--url=ws://localhost:8010/acp/ws"
      ]
    }
  }
}

Use the full path to the xah executable if the IDE cannot find it on its process PATH. See JetBrains' ACP setup guide for details.

In Zed, open Agent Settings → External Agents → Add Agent → Add Custom Agent; Zed opens the active settings file. On macOS and Linux without a custom XDG_CONFIG_HOME, it is typically ~/.config/zed/settings.json. Merge this entry into the existing JSON settings object:

{
  "agent_servers": {
    "xah": {
      "type": "custom",
      "command": "xah",
      "args": [
        "acp",
        "--url=ws://localhost:8010/acp/ws"
      ],
      "env": {}
    }
  }
}

Zed starts the proxy process; the xah server must still be running separately. Use dev: open acp logs from the command palette to inspect ACP messages if a connection fails. See Zed's external agents guide.

docs.title: Paths, instructions, and skills
docs.text:
xah keeps user data separate from project instructions and skills. Its defaults are:

Purpose Default path User data home ~/.xah/ ACP session store ~/.xah/sessions/ User-level agent instructions ~/.xah/.agents/AGENTS.md User-level skills ~/.xah/.agents/skills/ Project-level instructions <working directory>/.agents/AGENTS.md Project-level skills <working directory>/.agents/skills/

Project paths are based on the working directory supplied by the ACP client when it creates a session. xah reads user and project AGENTS.md files when present. It discovers skills in both skills folders; a project skill takes precedence when an ID appears in both. Session data is stored under the user data home.

You can customize these locations through the path settings. home changes where sessions and user-level files are stored; agents_dir and skills_dir choose the instruction and skills folders; agents_name changes the instruction filename. These settings are defined by PathAgent in xah/settings.py.

docs.title: Skills
docs.text:
Skills use the Agent Skills format: a folder containing SKILL.md, with YAML frontmatter for name and description, followed by Markdown instructions. For example, save this file as .agents/skills/python/style/SKILL.md:

---
name: style
description: Conventions for Python code in this project.
---

# Python style

Prefer clear names and small, direct changes.

The name is required metadata and, under the Agent Skills specification, should match the skill folder's name (style in this example). When skills are nested, xah identifies them by their path relative to the skills folder, such as python/style; use that ID when listing or loading a skill. User-level skills go under ~/.xah/.agents/skills/ instead.

AGENTS.md is separate from a skill: use it for instructions that should apply to every relevant session, and use skills for detailed guidance that can be discovered and loaded when needed.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text: Install xah, start its agent server, and connect an ACP client.

docs.title: Start the server
docs.text:
Install with pipRun with uv 
pip install xah
xah

uvx xah

The server listens on localhost:8010 by default. Leave it running while you use the client.

Set your OpenAI API key

xah uses OpenAI's gpt-6-luna model by default. Set the OPENAI_API_KEY environment variable before sending a prompt. If you use a different provider or model, configure its credentials instead.

Connect an ACP client

xah starts an agent server, not a chat window. An ACP client is the user-facing app where you choose an agent, send messages, and view replies. Clients are most often IDEs or editors, but desktop, terminal, and web interfaces are available too. See client setup.

For custom agents and tools, work through the tutorials.
• Initial release.
• First public release.

docs.title: Tutorials
docs.text: Start with the intro to build a minimal harness, then follow the tools tutorials to add custom capabilities.

docs.title: Intro
docs.text: Build your first custom agent in Build a minimal harness, then continue to the tools tutorials.

docs.title: Build a minimal harness
docs.text:
Start with a minimal agent and give it a simple purpose. This exercise creates an agent that responds only with “Hello World.”

from xah import Harness


class HelloWorld(Harness):
    # (1)!
    instructions = 'You are an agent who only says "Hello World"!'


if __name__ == "__main__":
    HelloWorld.launch()
  1. This instruction is what makes the harness a Hello World agent; the harness otherwise keeps xah's default settings.

Install xah with pip install xah in the Python environment you will use, then run python -m xah.examples.m01.e01_hello to start the agent server. To chat with it, connect an ACP client. Continue with the tool tutorials to give an agent additional capabilities.

docs.title: Example output
docs.text:
This shortened sample shows xah's traffic log. The default harness starts with the Management-Activate and Management-List tools, which it can use to enable other toolsets.

agent: HelloWorld
event: setup
# (1)! Setup shows the instructions and tools available to the harness.
# (2)! The instruction controls how the model should respond.
instructions: |-
  You are an agent who only says "Hello World"!
tools:
# (3)! These management tools can enable other toolsets.
- Management-Activate
- Management-List
agent: HelloWorld
event: model-request
messages:
# (4)! The client sends the user's message to the model.
- kind: user-prompt
  content: hi!
agent: HelloWorld
event: model-response
messages:
# (5)! The model returns the agent's answer.
- kind: text
  content: Hello World
  1. Setup shows the instructions and tools available to the harness.
  2. The instruction tells the model to answer only with “Hello World.”
  3. The default harness starts with management tools, which can activate other toolsets.
  4. The request contains the user's prompt.
  5. The response contains the model's final text.

docs.title: Tools tutorials
docs.text:
Work through these exercises to build a harness with a custom tool. Start with a single tool, group it into a toolset, and connect it to a harness. Then extend the example by adapting a tool and changing which capabilities the harness offers.

  • Define a tool
  • Group tools in a toolset
  • Make a toolset available to a harness
  • Customize a tool by subclassing
  • Add and remove tools

docs.title: Add and remove tools
docs.text:
This final exercise revisits the harness and toolset from the earlier examples, changing the capability the agent offers. It demonstrates how to evolve the available tools as an agent's purpose changes.

from xah.examples.m02.e01_tool import AgeTool
from xah.examples.m02.e02_toolset import UserFactsToolset
from xah.examples.m02.e03_harness import DemoHarness
from xah.examples.m02.e04_subclassing import PetTool


# (1)!
UserFactsToolset.Tools.append(PetTool)

# (2)!
UserFactsToolset.Tools.remove(AgeTool)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    DemoHarness.launch()
  1. Add PetTool to the toolset so DemoHarness can use it.
  2. Remove AgeTool to leave only the pet lookup tool available.

Install xah with pip install xah in the Python environment you will use, then run python -m xah.examples.m02.e05_adding and ask what pet a user has. The agent can now call UserFactsToolset-PetTool; this sample is illustrative, and a real run may choose a different pet.

docs.title: Example output
docs.text:
agent: DemoHarness
event: setup
# (1)! Setup confirms that AgeTool was replaced by PetTool.
# (2)! The harness keeps the same instruction while using the replacement tool.
instructions: Use the tools to tell the user facts about themself.
tools:
# (3)! Setup confirms that PetTool is now available instead of AgeTool.
- UserFactsToolset-PetTool
agent: DemoHarness
event: model-request
messages:
# (4)! The user's question is sent to the model.
- kind: user-prompt
  content: What pet does Maya have?
agent: DemoHarness
event: model-response
messages:
# (5)! The model calls the replacement tool.
- kind: tool-call
  tool_name: UserFactsToolset-PetTool
  args:
    user: Maya
agent: DemoHarness
event: tool-result
# (6)! The return value shows the result from the newly added tool.
kind: tool-return
tool_name: UserFactsToolset-PetTool
outcome: success
content: Maya has an otter as a pet.
agent: DemoHarness
event: model-response
messages:
- kind: text
  content: Maya has an otter as a pet.
  1. Setup shows that AgeTool was removed and PetTool is available.
  2. The harness keeps its instruction while the available tool changes.
  3. Setup records the replacement tool.
  4. The request contains the user's question.
  5. The model calls PetTool with Maya's name.
  6. The tool returns the pet for the model to use.

docs.title: Make a toolset available to a harness
docs.text:
This exercise connects the toolset from Group tools in a toolset to a harness, bringing the earlier examples together into an agent that can use the custom capability.

from xah import Harness, classes
from xah.examples.m02.e02_toolset import UserFactsToolset


class DemoHarness(Harness):
    instructions = "Use the tools to tell the user facts about themself."

    @classes
    def Toolsets(cls):
        # (1)!
        return [UserFactsToolset]


if __name__ == "__main__":
    DemoHarness.launch()
  1. This declaration replaces the default toolsets. Add any built-in or custom toolsets you also want the harness to have available.

Install xah with pip install xah in the Python environment you will use, then run python -m xah.examples.m02.e03_harness to start the agent server, then connect an ACP client. With the tool available, the model can request an age and use its result in a reply. This sample log shows the flow; actual ages and wording vary.

docs.title: Example output
docs.text:
agent: DemoHarness
event: setup
# (1)! Setup shows the custom instruction and tool exposed by the harness.
# (2)! The harness passes this instruction to the model.
instructions: Use the tools to tell the user facts about themself.
tools:
# (3)! The toolset makes this tool available to the model.
- UserFactsToolset-AgeTool
agent: DemoHarness
event: model-request
messages:
# (4)! The user's prompt is sent to the model.
- kind: user-prompt
  content: How old am I? My name is Maya.
agent: DemoHarness
event: model-response
messages:
# (5)! The model asks the harness to run the age tool.
- kind: tool-call
  tool_name: UserFactsToolset-AgeTool
  args:
    user: Maya
agent: DemoHarness
event: tool-result
# (6)! The tool's return value is logged so the model can use it.
kind: tool-return
tool_name: UserFactsToolset-AgeTool
outcome: success
content: Maya is 34 years old.
agent: DemoHarness
event: model-response
messages:
- kind: text
  content: Maya, you're 34 years old.
  1. Setup shows the custom instruction and tool exposed by the harness.
  2. The harness passes its instruction to the model.
  3. The toolset makes AgeTool available.
  4. The request contains the user's question.
  5. The model calls AgeTool with Maya's name.
  6. The tool returns the age for the model to use.

docs.title: Customize a tool by subclassing
docs.text:
This exercise builds on the age lookup by introducing a second kind of response while reusing the existing tool's foundation. It shows how to adapt an example for a new purpose without repeating its setup.

from random import choice

from xah.examples.m02.e01_tool import AgeTool


# (1)!
class PetTool(AgeTool):
    """Return a randomly chosen pet for a user."""

    # (2)!
    async def run(self):
        pet = choice(["cat", "otter", "axolotl"])
        return f"{self.user} has a {pet} as a pet."
  1. Because PetTool uses the same user argument as AgeTool, subclassing reuses its definition instead of duplicating it.
  2. Override run() to change the behavior while retaining the inherited argument.

The next exercise launches a harness that uses this subclass.

docs.title: Define a tool
docs.text:
This exercise introduces the basic shape of a custom tool through a small example that answers a question about a user. It demonstrates how to connect an agent-facing purpose to behavior that returns a result for the agent to use.

from random import randint

from pydantic import Field

from xah import Tool


class AgeTool(Tool):
    """Use this tool to provide a randomly generated age for a named user."""
    # (1)!

    # (2)!
    user: str = Field(
        ...,
        description="The name of the user whose age you want to know.",  # (3)!
    )

    async def run(self):
        # (4)!
        age = randint(1, 100)
        return f"{self.user} is {age} years old."
  1. The tool docstring is exposed to the agent, so use it to explain when and why it should call the tool.
  2. Tools are Pydantic AI models and support Python type annotations and Pydantic Fields.
  3. Field descriptions are also exposed to the agent and provide guidance for each argument.
  4. The harness calls run() when the model selects the tool; its return value is provided back to the model.

This file defines the tool used by the following toolset and harness exercises; it is not a standalone agent to launch.

docs.title: Group tools in a toolset
docs.text:
This exercise groups the tool from Define a tool into a toolset, creating a reusable collection of related capabilities for an agent.

from xah import Toolset, classes
from xah.examples.m02.e01_tool import AgeTool


class UserFactsToolset(Toolset):
    """Tools for fetching facts about users."""

    @classes
    def Tools(cls):
        # (1)!
        return [AgeTool]
  1. The toolset exposes each tool class listed here to the agent.

This toolset is connected to an agent in Make a toolset available to a harness. The sample output below shows what a run of that harness looks like when it uses the grouped tool.

docs.title: Example output
docs.text:
agent: DemoHarness
event: setup
# (1)! Setup shows the tool that the harness made available.
# (2)! This instruction tells the model when to use the tool.
instructions: Use the tools to tell the user facts about themself.
tools:
# (3)! The toolset contributes this tool to the model's available tools.
- UserFactsToolset-AgeTool
agent: DemoHarness
event: model-request
messages:
# (4)! The model receives the user's question.
- kind: user-prompt
  content: How old am I? My name is Maya.
agent: DemoHarness
event: model-response
messages:
# (5)! The model chooses the age tool and supplies its argument.
- kind: tool-call
  tool_name: UserFactsToolset-AgeTool
  args:
    user: Maya
agent: DemoHarness
event: tool-result
# (6)! The tool returns a value for the model to use.
kind: tool-return
tool_name: UserFactsToolset-AgeTool
outcome: success
content: Maya is 34 years old.
agent: DemoHarness
event: model-response
messages:
# (7)! The model turns the tool result into a user-facing answer.
- kind: text
  content: Maya, you're 34 years old.
  1. Setup records the instruction and the tool made available by the toolset.
  2. The instruction gives the model the tool's purpose.
  3. The toolset exposes AgeTool under its harness-facing name.
  4. The request contains the user's question.
  5. The model calls the tool with Maya's name.
  6. The tool returns the generated age.
  7. The model uses that result in its answer.
